syllabusTopics: Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes): preparation from haloalkanes (reduction and Wurtz reaction), decarboxylation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkene and alkyne
Chemical properties of alkanes: substitution reactions (halogenation, nitration and sulphonation only), oxidation of ethane
Unsaturated hydrocarbons (Alkenes): preparation by dehydration of alcohol, dehydrohalogenation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkyne
Chemical properties of alkenes: addition reaction with HX (Markovnikov's addition and peroxide effect), H2O, O3, H2SO4 only
Alkynes: preparation from carbon and hydrogen, 1,2-dibromoethane, chloroform/iodoform only
Chemical properties of alkynes: addition reaction with H2, HX, H2O; acidic nature (action with sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3 and ammoniacal Cu2Cl2)
Test of unsaturation (ethene and ethyne): bromine water test and Baeyer's test
Comparative studies of physical properties of alkane, alkene and alkyne
Kolbe's electrolysis methods for the preparation of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are non-polar, water-insoluble, less dense than water; boiling points rise with chain length and, at equal carbon number, with unsaturation."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Two butanes, two boiling points*** — same formula C4H10, five kelvin apart in boiling: the branched isomer simply offers less skin for its neighbours to grip.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Gases C1-4, liquids C5-17, solids C18+. B.p. ladder at same n: alkyne > alkene > alkane (C3+). Branching lowers b.p. Float on water; dissolve in benzene/ether. Smoky flame = high C% = alkyne.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Physical properties are contact accounting: more surface and more polarisable electrons mean stronger dispersion forces — chain length raises them, branching and small size lower them.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: C1-C4 gases, C5-C17 liquids, C18+ solids; all odourless when pure. B.p./m.p. rise with carbon number; at same n (C3+): alkyne > alkene > alkane (pi polarisability); branching lowers b.p. (n-butane -0.5C > isobutane -11.7C); C2 anomaly: ethene -104C < ethane -89C.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Oil floats on water for the same reason hydrocarbons refuse to dissolve in it: density below 1 g/cm3 and no polar handle for water's hydrogen bonds to grab.

Common Confusions **The C₂ anomaly:** ethene boils below ethane (−104 vs −89 °C) despite more unsaturation — small-molecule packing quirks; the alkyne ≥ alkene > alkane ladder is reliable from C₃ upward.  ·  **Branching beats unsaturation:** a branched alkane can boil lower than a straight alkene of the same formula — surface area matters as much as π.
